hero.heading: Andrea Ghidara, full stack web developer
hero.claim: Your website, cut to fit your company.
hero.subclaim: Measurements first: what you sell, and to whom. Then a site that explains, a store that sells, a platform that gets the work done.

sites.title: Sites and landing pages
sites.description: No bought themes filled with text. It starts from what a visitor has to understand in the first three seconds; structure, words and images follow from that. Then speed and indexing: the difference between having a site and being found.

ecommerce.title: E-commerce
ecommerce.description: I connect the catalogue to what you already run (back office, warehouse, courier) instead of asking you to update two systems by hand. Payments and shipping stay configurable: tomorrow you can switch provider without rebuilding the shop.

webapp.title: Web apps and platforms
webapp.description: We start from the smallest version that stands up and put it in front of a real person early. Roles, permissions and subscriptions get built from the start: adding them later means rewriting.

ai.title: AI and automation
ai.description: Connected to your real data, not to a model that guesses. And one rule I don't negotiate: when the assistant doesn't know, it hands over to a person instead of inventing an answer.

services.stageLead: A finished website. From here on, everything underneath it.
services.blank: And yours, what is it? Write to me.
services.punch: What you call «a website» is the screen in the middle. The rest is the work behind it.

site.title: The site
site.lead: What you see. Colour, type, hierarchy, words, images. And how all of it holds up on a six-inch screen.

logic.title: The logic
logic.lead: What the site does. Everything a visitor can do is a written rule, an edge case anticipated, an error handled before it happens.

infra.title: The infrastructure
infra.lead: What keeps it standing at three in the morning. You never see it, until it's missing. And then it's all you see.

growth.title: The services
growth.lead: What makes it grow after launch. A site going live is where the work starts, not where it's delivered.

comune.barrette: The four levels of the game

righe.schermo: First build the screen: colours, type, sections. Then unscrew it and see what's underneath.
righe.logiche: Behind the screen an order crosses six pieces of logic, and you move it on at each node. Or try to break the site.
righe.pannello: The site is live. A month after launch, in one minute: the lights come on, and someone steps in.
righe.notte: What keeps the site up even at three in the morning. It's set up in advance, and seen only when missing.
righe.finale: That's the whole round. Use the bars above to reopen any level.

stili.cosa: How it looks and how it moves.

mezzo.cosa: How front end and back end talk, and the fast memory between them.

back.cosa: The rules: who can do what, and what happens when they do.

auth.cosa: Who you are, and what you are allowed to do.

dati.cosa: Where the things that must not be lost are kept.

nextjs.cosa: The framework: pages rendered on the server or on demand, routing, server actions.

react.cosa: The pieces of the interface, and their state.

tailwind.cosa: Styles written next to the markup, on one scale of sizes.

shadcn-ui.cosa: Accessible components copied into the project, not a library to keep updating.

gsap.cosa: Scroll-driven animation, accurate to the frame.

framer-motion.cosa: Animation for React components: entrances and exits.

radix.cosa: The accessible behaviour under shadcn: focus, keyboard, ARIA.

graphql.cosa: Ask only for the data you need, all at once.

rest.cosa: The simplest APIs: one address per resource.

trpc.cosa: Call the back end like a function, with shared types.
trpc.breve: the back end as a function

redis.cosa: Fast memory: cache, queues, sessions, rate limits.

websocket.cosa: A line that stays open, for what changes in real time.

nodejs.cosa: JavaScript outside the browser: the engine under the whole back end.

express.cosa: The minimal back end: routes and middleware, nothing more.

nestjs.cosa: The structured back end: modules, dependency injection, decorators.

authjs.cosa: NextAuth: sign-in inside the Next app, with the providers you want.

supabase-auth.cosa: Sign-in next to the database, with row-level policies.

jwt.cosa: The signed token that says who you are on every request.

postgresql.cosa: The reference relational database: transactions, constraints, extensions.

mongodb.cosa: Documents instead of tables, when the schema changes often.

prisma.cosa: The ORM: the schema in one file, typed queries.

drizzle.cosa: The lightweight ORM, close to SQL.

vercel.cosa: The front end at the edge, close to whoever opens it.
vercel.breve: the front end at the edge

railway.cosa: Servers, databases and Redis without managing machines.

docker.cosa: The same environment from my computer to production.

typescript.cosa: Types, from the browser to the database: if data changes shape, I find out first.

vitest.cosa: Tests: what has to keep working, written down.

zod.cosa: Validation: the same schema checks the form and the API.

langchain.cosa: Connects the model to documents and tools.

works.title: Four projects, and how they were run
works.intro: Four real projects. For each one: what the job was, the solution I chose and why that one, and how the work was run through to delivery.

labels.riporta: bring this folder to the front
labels.comEra: How it was when I arrived

riservato.name: Under NDA
riservato.riga: A fitness business working with several outside tools, each with its own subscription.
riservato.lavoro: Several clients, in different markets. The biggest project is a platform for fitness: with a small team we brought the tools the business already used into one place.
riservato.scelta: Bring what came from the outside subscriptions into the platform, so that clients, contracts and commissions all sit in the same place.
riservato.conduzione: We took the tools the business was using, looked at which features the client actually needed, and brought them onto our platform, tuned more closely to their needs.

bdroppy.name: BDroppy
bdroppy.riga: The platform was on Next 14, with much of the code still in JavaScript, and the shipping pages were slow because they weren't well optimised: that's where we started, optimising them.
bdroppy.lavoro: Upgrade the platform from Next 14 to Next 15, improve its performance and fix the bugs it had been carrying.
bdroppy.scelta: Move the code towards TypeScript wherever possible, instead of rewriting it all. Legacy JavaScript stays where it works, and new or touched parts are typed from the start.
bdroppy.conduzione: Upgrade, performance and interface in the same job: we reworked the product selection and checkout screens, to make finding a product and buying it simpler.

aidify.name: Aidify
aidify.riga: Shopify stores that had to answer customers at any hour, even when nobody was in front of the screen.
aidify.lavoro: An AI chatbot that handles customer support inside Shopify stores, and the landing page that brings stores to try it, then to stay.
aidify.scelta: A single widget that adapts to each store: style and colours change to fit in, without touching the code.
aidify.conduzione: By optimising the widget on Shopify so it wouldn't weigh down the store hosting it, and by looking after the landing page for acquiring and retaining customers and leads.

visualboost.name: VisualBoost
visualboost.riga: A service that creates AI images of a store's products: a showcase made almost entirely of images, which had to open instantly.
visualboost.lavoro: The service's landing page and the loading of the images, which here are the product itself.
visualboost.scelta: Work on the images before the code: the right formats and sizes, and loading only when they're needed.
visualboost.conduzione: Measuring with Lighthouse before and after, with an eye on conversion: a page that opens instantly is a page that gets read down to the button.

process.title: How we can carry on
process.intro: It isn't a rulebook, it's a convenience: four moments agreed up front, so neither of us has to ask the other where we are. If your case wants a different order, we change it.

documento.quando: Within 48 hours of the first meeting
documento.lead: Two pages: what the project needs, and how long each piece takes.

dentro.uno: The basics we need before we can start
dentro.due: What's essential to go live, and what can wait
dentro.tre: What's worth leaving out, or turning into something else

documento.nonlo: It's the project's instruction booklet: from there on it's only a matter of building it.
documento.perche: We can write it together: if something needs changing, this is the moment when changing it is cheap.

schermo.quando: Before a single line of code exists
schermo.lead: The screens that matter, before they exist. Not all of them: only the ones where somebody decides something.

dentro.uno: The screen where someone who doesn't know you lands
dentro.due: The one where somebody buys, books or writes
dentro.tre: The one you'll use yourself, every day, for years

schermo.nonlo: It isn't finished design, and it's black and white on purpose: colour gets discussed later, order gets discussed now.
schermo.perche: We make the important decisions looking at this, together. Changing a drawing costs an afternoon; changing something already built costs a week.

link.quando: Every two weeks, until the end
link.titolo: A link where you can look and try
link.lead: Not a screenshot and not a presentation: an address you open on your phone while the work goes on.

dentro.uno: You can click around inside it
dentro.due: You can show it to a colleague without explaining it
dentro.tre: You can reject it, which is exactly why I give it to you

link.nonlo: It isn't a release. It's the same thing, incomplete, but real: what's there actually works.
link.perche: It's the difference between finding a problem two weeks in and finding it two days from the end.

numero.quando: From launch on, with no end date
numero.lead: After launch a person answers, and the person is me. Not a ticket, not a form, not another supplier.

dentro.uno: Fixes: if I broke it, I fix it
dentro.due: Changes, quoted one at a time
dentro.tre: «Can this be done?», even when the answer is no

numero.nonlo: It isn't a support contract you have to sign. If you don't need it you don't pay for it, and if you do, you already know who to call.
numero.perche: It's a contact that stays with you, both for support and for the ideas that come later.

journey.title: Where I learned
journey.nota: Nobody hands you a badge when you work for yourself.

freelanceOggi.body: My own clients' projects, plus backing up other freelancers: from the dashboard that centralises a business to the small tools orbiting it.
freelanceOggi.lezione: How to talk to people who aren't technical: it's the skill I use more than any language. And the work I do now: moving a business from several tools onto a single platform, running video streaming for clients, holding documents and contracts together, letting many operators work on the same things at the same time.

dlab.role: Front-end Developer / UI and UX Designer
dlab.body: Four products, some the company's and some its clients': a B2B platform to migrate, an AI assistant, an image archive and an analytics platform.
dlab.lezione: I learned to sort the work and to be on several projects at once, deciding with the team what came first. And to build inside applications already in production, still billing every day: there, every change you make is made while somebody is buying.

eroi.body: E-commerce platforms across Vue and Laravel: interfaces, authentication, APIs and the panels people actually work in.
eroi.lezione: Holding several technologies together instead of using one at a time: Vue and Inertia on top of Laravel, with load times coming down because the two halves stop redoing each other's work. And the first grounding in authentication, which is where a site stops being a shop window.

freelanceInizio.body: First commissioned work: development and interface for a reselling business's dashboard.
freelanceInizio.lezione: I learned to work on a project that was already running, where I had to put the code in context, understand what each piece did and how the whole product logic was built, so I could implement what I was asked for.
